docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This subsystem monitors environmental conditions using digital sensors for soil moisture, rainwater, and temperature/humidity. It uses a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller to read sensor data via analog pins and digital I/O and PWM which processes the information and makes it available to the rest of the system for decision-making.

The system is powered by a 9V, 3A unregulated power supply and is regulated down to 5V, 1.5A using a voltage regulator to ensure safe and stable operation of the microcontroller and all connected sensors.

It interfaces with three digital sensors: -Soil Moisture Sensor -Rain Water Sensor -Temperature/Humidity Sensor

Actuator Interface: This subsystem doesn't directly control an actuator but it provides sensor data to other subsystems such as motor control that can act upon the readings.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text: Subsystem board powered from 9 V input through a 5 V regulator. Includes a PIC18F16Q41 Curiosity Nano microcontroller connected to: - Analog soil moisture sensor - Temperature/humidity sensor - Rain sensor - 8-pin connector to communicate with other boards

docs.title: Soil Moisture Sensor (Analog)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Resistive probe (e.g., YL-69 Module)$2 eachYL-69 Resistive Sensor Very low costEasy analog output for ADC Corrodes quicklyNon-linear readingsRequires frequent calibration Option 2: Capacitive soil moisture sensor v1.2$5 eachCapacitive Soil Module No corrosionStable analog signalCompact size Slightly higher costNeeds calibration per soil type Option 3: Industrial analog soil moisture transmitter (4–20 mA output)$22 eachIndustrial Soil Transmitter Weatherproof housingHighly accurate and robust ExpensiveLarger form factor

Choice: Option 2 — Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor v1.2 Rationale: Provides stable analog readings without corrosion, suitable for long-term outdoor deployment while remaining low-cost and easy to interface with the PIC ADC.

docs.title: Temperature & Humidity Sensor
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: DHT22 / AM2302$6 eachDHT22 Sensor Low costEasy to use (library support) Slow sampling rateModerate accuracy Option 2: SHT31-D (I²C)$12 eachSHT31-D Sensor High accuracy and stabilityFast responseI²C communication Higher price Option 3: BME280 (I²C/SPI)$14 eachBME280 Sensor Adds pressure measurementAccurate & low power Adds unnecessary feature (pressure)Slightly more expensive

Choice: Option 2 — SHT31-D Sensor Rationale: Best balance of precision, low power, and easy I²C integration for the PIC18F16Q41.

docs.title: Rain Sensor
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Analog rain detection board (YL-83)$3 eachYL-83 Rain Module Cheap and simpleAnalog or digital output Corrodes over timeNot weatherproof Option 2: Optical rain sensor (IR reflection type)$25 eachOptical Rain Sensor Non-contact detectionLong life Requires optical calibrationHigher cost Option 3: Tipping-bucket rain gauge$60 eachTipping Bucket Sensor Accurate rainfall measurement (mm) Bulky, mechanical partsRequires mounting and calibration

Choice: Option 1 — YL-83 Analog Rain Module Rationale: Simple analog detection is sufficient for moisture-triggered irrigation logic and is easy to interface with PIC ADC inputs.

docs.title: Voltage Regulator (9 V → 5 V)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: LM7805 Linear Regulator$1 eachLM7805 Simple circuit, low noiseStable 5 V output Inefficient (heat loss) when dropping from 9 V Option 2: LM2596 Buck Converter$4 eachLM2596 Buck Module Efficient, handles higher currentCool operation More switching noise (may need filtering)

Choice: Option 1 — LM7805 Linear Regulator Rationale: Estimated system current is low; LM7805 gives a clean, low-noise 5 V rail which benefits ADC readings from analog sensors. If measured current grows above ~200–300 mA, switch to a buck converter.

docs.title: Microcontroller (PIC18F16Q41 Curiosity Nano)  (subsystem: MCU)
docs.text:
• Board: Microchip Curiosity Nano with PIC18F16Q41
  • Notes: Use the Curiosity Nano breakout footprint or include the bare PIC18F16Q41 on your PCB as your design requires.
  • Power/IO: 5 V logic (confirm board configuration) and ADC inputs for soil and rain sensors; I²C for SHT31.

Rationale for selection: PIC18F16Q41 provides sufficient analog inputs, low-power operation options, and easy integration with Microchip Curiosity Nano development board for rapid prototyping and debugging.

Important: Replace the estimated current values in your power budget with the PIC18F16Q41 absolute maximum current values from the Microchip datasheet and the Curiosity Nano board documentation (required for accuracy in the power budget).

docs.title: +5 V Rail
docs.text:
• Subtotal (estimated) = 82 mA
  • Safety margin (25%) → 82 × 1.25 = 102.5 mA → round to 103 mA

docs.title: Section C – Regulator Selection
docs.text:
Regulator Option Input Range (V) Max Output (mA) Pros Cons LM7805 (linear) 7 – 35 V 1000 Low noise, simple Inefficient (dissipates (9–5)V × I) LM2596 (buck) 6 – 40 V 2000 High efficiency, low heat Switching noise; filter may be required

Choice: LM7805 Linear Regulator Rationale: With estimated 103 mA load the dissipation is ≈ 4 V × 0.103 A = 0.412 W — acceptable without a large heatsink. LM7805 gives a clean rail which benefits analog readings. If measured final current > 200–300 mA, switch to a buck regulator.

Battery option example: 9 V alkaline ~500 mAh - Battery life ≈ Capacity / Load = 500 mAh / 103 mA ≈ 4.85 hours (worst-case)

docs.title: How to finalize
docs.text:
1. Open the PIC18F16Q41 datasheet / Curiosity Nano documentation.
  2. Find absolute maximum current values for the MCU (active modes, peripherals enabled) and add any extra consumption from the Curiosity Nano board (USB interface, LEDs, onboard regulator) if you plan to use the development board.
  3. Replace the estimate in Section A and recompute totals in Sections B–E.
  4. If final current > ~200–300 mA, switch the regulator choice to a buck converter and recalculate heat and battery life.
